title: Lebanon: Middle East Overview: July 2026
original_summary:
Countries: Lebanon, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Iraq, occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data

Remote violence events fell to their lowest level since the latest resumption of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah, dropping around 35% compared to May in Lebanon and approximately 70% in Israel. This decline follows the announcement of an agreement to implement a ‌ceasefire, reached during negotiations in Washington on 3 June. Despite the reduction, Lebanon remained one of the region’s most active conflict zones, with ongoing exchanges of artillery and rockets demonstrating that the ceasefire has diminished, but not resolved, hostilities.

Israeli military activities in Lebanon remained concentrated in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah maintains its primary military strongholds. The majority of Israeli strikes targeted the Tyr and Bint Jbeil districts, both south of the Litani River, as well as the al-Nabatieh region, north of the Litani River. Israel also announced in a statement on 11 June that, following days of clashes with Hezbollah, it had achieved operational control over Wadi Saluki, extending a security buffer around the Israeli communities of the Galilee Panhandle and Metula.

While Hezbollah attacks against northern Israel became less frequent, Hezbollah maintained sustained pressure on Israeli forces operating inside Lebanon in the Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun, and Tyr districts. The most significant incident occurred on 19 June, when Hezbollah launched a drone attack on an Israeli armored unit in Kfar Tebnit town, killing four Israeli soldiers, including the commander of the 401st Armored Brigade’s 52nd Battalion, and marking the deadliest attack against Israeli forces since the June ceasefire.

Diplomatic efforts gained momentum in late June, but the ceasefire remained fragile with repeated attacks by both sides. The US-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed on 17 June, helped to decrease regional tensions and was followed by a new round of Israel-Lebanon discussions in Washington on 22 June about withdrawal, border security, and Hezbollah's future role. While Israel has since lifted most civilian restrictions in northern Israel following the reduction in Hezbollah attacks, the current ceasefire is unlikely to evolve into a durable peace. Even under a broader political agreement, Hezbollah is unlikely to relinquish its military capabilities voluntarily, suggesting that Israeli military operations and localized hostilities in southern Lebanon are likely to persist.
